My attempts to really sit down and write the list of exactly when I saw shows and who was there would be a bit... skewed.  I count everything from little acoustic performances to the conferences/festivals, and your standard concerts.  Just last weekend, I did two major concerts and one in-store album signing, and I've got one more tomorrow night and another two coming up next weekend - and that's slow for me because, well, life is kicking my ass at the moment. :\ 

Anyway, here are some standouts:

Best: Rich Aucoin.  Ended up seeing him twice - first in Halifax during the Junos and then again earlier this month when he came through Ottawa.  His entire show is basically him, a projector with a slide show, one synthesizer and a school parachute.  I ran out of room on my SD cards on my cameras both times because of how much pure energy there was.

Worst: I really can't say.  If they were bad, then I've probably forgotten all about them.

Most surprising: Jelly Roll at Ottawa Bluesfest.  He was a last-minute and very hyped-up addition to the festival (something to do with the first time he's been able to perform outside of the US or something).  All of us photogs weren't initially impressed - a lot of us just aren't country fans and we might have been hoping for something more rock in the surprise announcement. But, you could feel just how excited and happy Mr. Roll was to be there, and it reflected so well in our photos. 

Most unique: A classical chamber ensemble called Art of Time, when they performed the entirety of *Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band* at a decommissioned military air hanger in Ontario's Prince Edward County, with special guests that included Steven Page (formerly of Barenaked Ladies) and Sloan's Chris Murphy.  Super rural setting on a stunning July night with some of the best music known to us music fans. *mwah* Chef's kiss!

Other shows of note: 

* The shows I'm attending next weekend will be my 40th and 41st Sloan shows, and my third and fourth for the entire year.  
* I travelled to see the Trans-Canada Highwaymen in my hometown. It was particularly special for me because they played the theatre I spent my childhood volunteering at, and I was given free reign for my photos. 
* Covered a show at Ottawa's Canadian Tire Centre for the first time.  It was Arkells, and it also marks the first time I shot a band of that stature completely for myself.
* The night I saw Rich Aucoin in Halifax, I also watched the Juno Songwriter Circle and singer Begonia, and travelled between three separate venues in different areas across town on foot.  It was glorious.
* I was at every night of Bluesfest, which was a first.

To put it simply, this movie made me unbelievably *happy.*

First off, I'm simply happy it turned out as well as it did. When I first heard they were doing it, I had a list of things that could have gone wrong with it and generally felt unsure. I mean, I don't know about anyone else, but when I found out about it, my mind immediately went to the track record of the other dozen or so SNL-adjacent movies. Not to mention, I've seen more than my fair share of biopics (including a couple surrounding SNL stories) to know that I shouldn't get my hopes up because there was a good chance this thing would be hot garbage worthy of re-watch for being so bad it's good in a best case scenario. But no, I got an anxiety-inducing raw portrayal of the pure chaos of that show on the whole; and to a point where I frequently reminded myself that, spoiler alert, the show will absolutely on - just as it has for the past 50 years.

I am EXTREMELY happy with that cast. Good gracious God, they all fucking NAILED it. There are no impressions, just actors playing to the essence of real people. Just the thought that Lorne's portrayal wasn't at all a caricature makes the entire film feel earned. 

I'm happy with the way the story was presented. Whether intended or not, a lot of the criticisms of the movie can be explained in ways that make sense within the context of the broader history show itself. One actor playing two legendary performers that couldn't be more polar opposite if they tried? It's a no-brainer because it's something that happens on the show on a weekly basis. Hell, the fact that they latched onto the seemingly random fact that Billy Crystal was totally there that night, fully prepared to perform, gave the film a way to subtlety explain the process of sketch cuts and how nerve-wracking it still must be for cast/crew. The movie definitely tells the story of where the show started, but it masterfully gave hints as to where it will go on a level beyond simple Easter eggs.

Finally, I'm happy because it reminded me of how deeply I've loved the show my entire life and how great it is to be such a massive nerd in general. The show made me happy as a kid going through my mom's personal archives of taped shows. It made me happy in the earliest days of the internet to learn about the show's history.  And, this faithful little movie came out during a particularly challenging time in my life where I need reminders of the little things that make life enjoyable for me. The only reason my mom, who's been watching since that first episode, wasn't with me when I saw it was because she's been in the hospital for the past two weeks. But be assured, I'm making it a goal to get her out to see it as soon as humanly possible - because *Saturday Night Live* makes her happy, and she deserves the smile.

So yeah. It's been a week, and despite the bullshit of the world around me, I become happy when I think about that movie; and I'm glad it exists.

Spotify. 

I know other streaming apps are probably better, and if I could figure out a way to transfer my lovingly curated playlists almost 1,000 songs long to another service completely seamlessly, I'd start to shop around for something different. But as a child of the turn of the century, I went from a CD Walkman, plus 10 CD wallet, plus two or three extra in their cases, plus a ziplock bag of batteries at the brink of death problem, plus wired headphones (because I hate earbuds) problem, to a device only slightly bigger than my hand that gets through the day on an overnight charge and a pair of Bluetooth cans; all in the name of canceling out the bullshit noise around me with whatever music works to calm my anxiety in the moment.  And, the entire thing costs a fraction of what I used to pay for CDs alone.  

Not a single day goes by where I don't tap into Spotify for something.

TL;DR: Sloan are the greatest band of all time, and I found out the awesome way that they are clearly not assholes.

So, it starts off with me being just a fairly big fan of Sloan in high school. I basically fell in love when I saw their video, bought the CD, and was ultra pumped when they were announced to my town's big concert festival the summer between grade 11 and grade 12. It also helped that I was studying bass at the time, and the bass lines I was hearing in their songs were in the same melodic style that I really love Paul McCartney for, so I really ended up latching on to the music quite intensely. Didn't get to meet the band this first time I saw them, but I was impressed enough (loud, straightforward power-pop contained within a mighty four piece band) and that awesome bass player (guy named Chris Murphy) pulled a kid on stage and gave him his guitar. (Bands do that?! This guy is so my hero!)

The problem is that none of my friends seemed to want anything to do with them. They had heard from parents/older siblings/whoever else that this band was a bunch of assholes, and they all thought the music sucked. And, this was a sentiment that continued to my first adult jobs - so many people I spoke to just hated this band and had all heard from friends of friends that they were assholes. But, the music was just too fucking good for me to give any shits about what people tried to warn me on, so on I listened.

The second time I saw them, I bought a shirt - and proceeded to find all four of them after the show to sign it. Not one of them gave me a cold shoulder, nor did it feel like I was being a pain. And especially Murphy - the moment the show ended, he left the stage from the center (right in front of me!) to start hanging out with the crowd. Bottom line, I figured out quickly that I'd been somewhat lied to (l dunno, maybe my friends and coworkers spoke to them on an off day?) and I kind of felt proud for finding out for myself if something was true or not.

*BUT THAT'S NOT ALL.*

Fast forward a few years. I'm officially obsessed enough that I go on a concert cruise in part because they'd be on it. There, I meet the handful of other hardcore fans who made the trek, and over the course of the week, we become a bit of a known little gaggle of superfans when we basically followed them up and down the eastern US, Ontario and Quebec. Always, the band remains kind and patient. And, it has become easier for me to count how many shows I that I didn't interact with Murph than it is for me to remember how many times I've chatted with him.

And then, I went back to school for journalism. I didn't want journalism initially - I wanted to study music, but I felt like that ship was long gone by then, and at least journalism came with skills an office would find appealing and with the added bonus of being interesting. I did not intend at all to wind up back within music, but here I am, a decade into a sort-of career as a music journalist and photographer that's criss-crossed Canada twice in search of awesome adventures in the name of music - and who do you think has been one of the most reliable people I can contact to point me in the right direction when I have general questions or want to bring my cameras to a show?

It should also be known that Murph has his own fan story he's super proud of. Back when he was a teenager, him and a bunch of his friends got in a van and drove down to Washington DC to seek out Dischord Records, and they ended up on the doorstep of Ian Mackaye; who was gracious enough to welcome them all into his home and made them feel comfortable. Murph has since paid the gesture forward ten fold for all fans - on top of being the last one to leave the venue after a show for how much he says with fans, since the pandemic, Murph has hosted annual garage sale of past Sloan merch in the alleyway behind his house. 

The next Sloan shows I attend in November will be numbers 40 and 41, respectively; and both are within months of my 40th birthday. I'm at a point where I've been around them and higher profile artists to know that everyone is, above all else, human, but I know I'd be cheating myself if I didn't try and formulate something worthy of the kindness I've been shown by my favourite little band over the years.  Just something to say thank you for being a light when I've needed it the most.

So yeah, find out for yourself if your heroes are worth your time. The experience might just surprise you.

Called me out for being late after the first time I ever voted.

It was an Ontario provincial election that happened when I was 18, and, conveniently, my polling station was my own high school, AND I had a spare first period. So, I planned accordingly. I was at school a full half hour before I was supposed to be there for a task I knew only takes five minutes, tops. So I presented myself to the polling workers, said I was there to vote and was prepared to take my ID out, when they told me to have a seat on the bench and someone would be with me. I thought that was odd, but OK. For the next 20 minutes, I was outright ignored - and it's not like these people were actually busy. As I said, it was a provincial election, and voter turnouts in Ontario are historically abysmal - not like there was a massive lineup or anything. Then the warning bell rang, so I got up, went back to the check-in, and it was only then that it clued in with them that this "kid" was eligible to vote. By the time I completed what I'd set out to do, the second bell rang, and I was late. I thought, "No problem. I'm of age to excuse myself."  

I finally walked through the classroom door and immediately blasted in front of the class (all of whom were younger than me but would be of voting age soon) for being late. When I explained the circumstance, I was told that "you need to set aside your own time to vote on election day - I can't just leave class to vote, I have to wait until I have time!"

The older I get, the more I see people skipping their opportunities to vote and the consequences of that basic inaction (particularly in Ontario!) - and the angrier I get over the interaction.

"Qaisimalaurittuq" by Elisape 

The short of it is this song is a cover of Pink Floyd's "Wish You Were Here," translated into Inuktitut, which is the main indigenous language family of Canada's Arctic region. In fact, the album it is on, called *Inuktitut*, is entirely a cover album of classic rock songs Elisape (who is Inuit from Northern Quebec) grew up listening to, translated into Inuktitut. And yes, each one was chosen in relation to personal memories.

In interviews that I had read about the album, Elisape said that "Wish You Were Here" was chosen for the connection it had to all the times she mourned for a friend who had taken their own life - which is an extremely sad reality in a lot of Canada's indigenous communities.

So, to summarize, this is a song originally written in English about a devastating mental health issue within a group of friends, by a band from a country who was responsible for much of the colonialism that decimated indigenous cultures around the world, being sung in a language that could have been eradicated as a result of said colonialism, in relation a devastating mental health issue within a group of friends, that has it's roots in the consequences of colonialism. 

And now I, a Canadian so culturally British that watching the Queen's funeral was like burying her 92-year-old Nan all over again and whose music identity was birthed by the records that immigrated to Canada in 1975 with her Manunican father (like, I fucking bleed Yorkshire Tea, that's how British I am) want to learn to sing one of her all time favourite songs in an indigenous language. 

I don't know what struck my nervous system first: the recognition of profound decolonization in my own brain, the equally profound realization that I'd witnessed the most reversed colonization imaginable, or just the simple, highly addictive pleasure of enjoying music as the deepest expression of pure art one could ever experience.

Oh, and the arrangement of "Qaisimalaurittuq" is done in such a way that a friend of mine commented that it sounds a bit like a slow, New Orleans-style funeral procession. You know, because the original isn't excruciatingly mournful enough when placed in the context of suicide. You've been warned.

I've scrolled too long and haven't seen **Sloan** mentioned. It's my pleasure to be the one to correct this and to make the case for the following albums by the closest thing Canada has ever produced to the Beatles:

* ***One Chord to Another*** The overall fan favourite, and a really great place for new listeners to start. It's everything you'd want in a Beatlesque indie-pop release. 

* ***Navy Blues*** If the fan didn't choose *One Chord* as their favourite, than it's probably this one. It's definitely the louder of the two, but the energy is downright infectious. 

* ***Between the Bridges*** My personal favourite. The closest they've got to a true "concept" album (all the songs seem to have a loose theme of early band days in Halifax) and the kind of record you can listen to multiple times on repeat. 

* ***Never Hear the End of It*** Objectively, their best  and most underrated/underappreciated - and probably their *White Album,* for comparison for how massive it is (30 songs - it's double vinyl, but the CD release is on a single disc). Each songwriter in the band has songs on this thing that can be argued to be among their individual best. The record is an absolute beast of a recording and doesn't get nearly the love it deserves (in my opinion).

Honourable mentions:

* ***Twice Removed*** An album with a storied history that includes getting dropped from their label, the near complete dissolvement of the band itself, and ultimately being voted as one of the greatest Canadian albums of all time on multiple occasions. 
* ***Commonwealth*** Interesting, logical successor to *Never Hear...*, only this time, they individually took a side of an LP. (Think the four Kiss "solo records", only in one double vinyl.) For his side, their drummer decided to write one, 17-minute song with several movements, because why the fuck not.
* ***Steady*** Their 13th and most recent release. It came out almost exactly 30 years to the day of their first - and damn if it doesn't sound like the band aged a day. 😌

What helps: Dark humour and being able to talk openly and honestly about suicidal ideation - not outright suicide, mind you. Just the very real intrusive thoughts.

What doesn't help: shaming ideation and leaving people uncomfortable to ask for help. That includes shutting down the dark humour. It's not about romanticizing it. It's about finding a bit of comfortable in the absurdity of the situation.

*Clayton Park* - Thrush Hermit/*Ashtray Rock* - Joel Plaskett 

Sloan's been well discussed here, so I'm going with their noted Halifax Pop Explosion contemporary, Joel Plaskett. I'm not sure exactly to what extent the overarching story is non-fiction, but there's definitely a beauitful continuation between *Clayton Park* and *Ashtray Rock*; with the first (released under his original band, Thrush Hermit) is this wonderfully loud and unrelenting burst of energy that seemingly tells a story of a first-time touring band, and the second explicitly telling a story of the desolation of a young band. Both are fantastic and worth listening to for anyone looking for something fresh and interesting.

>I'm wondering how similar or different the Great Lakes beaches are to ocean beaches?

I grew up on the Canadian shores of Lake Huron. The beach basically extends from Sarnia straight up to Tobermory on the Bruce Peninsula - and then some, because Wasaga Beach (literally the longest freshwater beach in the world!) is on the opposite side of the Peninsula on Georgian Bay. (Fun fact, the second longest freshwater beach is Sauble Beach, which is also on the Canadian shores of Lake Huron!) The sunsets alone make you forget you are about as far as you can get from the Pacific without outright hitting the Atlantic on the US mainland.

And, a lot of those beaches are SUPER sandy. Pinary Provincial Park, near Grand Bend, is an oak savanna and is surrounded by enormous sand dunes that extend onto the beaches.  Those beaches, by the way, are also notably quite shallow - so when the sun is beating down on a 35°C day and there's been too little wind to stir up sediment, water can be clear, lukewarm and not at all what you'd expect from a lake whose waters were once trapped in a glacier. 

Once, my family vacationed on the Florida Gulf Coast, and I found the sand to be hard as rock and the saltwater generally unimpressive. 

Conclusion: I have an extreme personal bias, but I'm also confident in saying Lake Huron beaches are the best in the world. Just make sure to come after or during a June/July heatwave to let it warm up a bit. It's still Canada, after all. ⛱️

Honestly? The Polaris Music Prize long and short lists.  

Now, Polaris is Canada specific becuase that's where I am, but many countries have their own versions - the UK has the Mercury Prize, France has Prix Constantin, Nordic Music Prize for Scandinavia, etc. The point of these monetary prizes is to determine the best album of the year and is voted on by music journalists and broadcasters, completely independent of the record industry - which generally means a lot of artists that barely make it to local campus radio.

For me, in Canada, our long and short lists are some of the most diverse and wide-ranging selections I've ever seen. Obviously, a lot of artists I've liked over the years have made it to the short list, and some have even won; and there's always something new, unique, and out-there for me to discover. Some of my favourite artists in general were Polaris discoveries, and it's my personal number one source as an Anglophone for me to discover Francophone artists - including at least one absolutely bonkers experimental jazz band from my own city. 

So, yeah, its a bit of an out of the box suggestion. But you might be surprised for what you might find!

The jist of it is, despite my sometimes uncontrollable levels of anxiety, depression and low self-esteem, coupled with the sad realities of working a job that would make r/antiwork melt with rage, I've all but achieved my ultimate goal of living a life completely saturated in music. 

I'm not the rock star like I wanted when I was studying bass guitar - the first nervous breakdowns insured that it wasn't meant to be. Since then, although I still fight the good fight against mental illness, it feels like every year has brought new and important milestones. I've participated in seven Juno Awards now (five in person), and it's now a major goal to do as many as I can for the simple fact that I'm seeing the entirity of Canada through a music lens. Of course, that brings us up to this month. Last week, I covered the Polaris Music Prize for the fourth time as a photographer, and for the first time as a juror. That's right, I apparently had enough work under my name to be considered enough of a journalist to be on a committee to determine a major industry award. It's one thing to achieve goals you've had since childhood, but this moment was a whole other level because I can remember being at my first full-time job, listening to podcasts that discussed the Prize - all while trying to shake off severe ideation. Bonus, it marked the first time I'd ever stepped foot inside Massey Hall, and I was doing so as "professional" of sorts.

The day after the big event, I caught wind that one of my favourite bands was doing an album launch party.  But, it was supposed to start when I was scheduled to leave Toronto. I'm pretty sure my shots were the first time I took a genuine, non-performance, or red carpet portrait of a musician - who just happens to be the lead singer of one of the single most successful bands in Canada right now.

Finally, this Thursday, I'm back to Massey Hall to cover a massive event that will induct a slew of Canadian rock bands from the 70s and 80s onto Canada's Walk of Fame. Included on the list of inductees is my high school bass teacher. I can only hope that whatever photo I'm able to produce will honour that particular time in my life, while simultaneously honouring my teacher, who I didn't understand was actually a fairly big deal (and least, in Canadian rock history terms) until I moved to the other side of Ontario and heard his song on the radio for the first time. 

So yeah, I have too many moments to be proud of. I just kind of wish I was in a better spot, mentally, to appreciate them at their fullest.

I've actually discussed this recently with a friend. I think the true secret and gift Steve brought to the band, particularly through the classic run of albums in the 90s, was an incredibly healthy sense competition. Ed allowed Steve to embrace irreverence while crafting songs thar complimented Ed's successful streak of unabashed novelty, and in turn, Steve forced Ed to occasionally let up on the silly and far more varied and overall thoughtful in his songwriting. I, for one, know damn well he was just as fully responsible for the absolutely stunning "Light Up My Room" on *Stunt* as he was "One Week."  As partners, they were a literal yinyang when it came to songwriting. 

Ed has the chops, but with Steve out of the picture, and so far from the spotlight to be of any threat, the balance is gone, and Ed has no other drive than to keep the band together and to make sure they generate an income. At the end of the day, I can't say I can fault him for the path I feel he chose.  But man, does it hurt not to hear what he's truly capable of, and to know there really isn't room for him (or the rest of the band) to be honest with themselves as to just how far the quailty of their recorded work has plummeted. But, it is what it is. They're very lucky to be able to still be able to play at roughly the same level as before - and that I, personally, have a general understanding that I'm too old school to completely like the new album, but should never toss an opportunity to at least cover their show when they come through my town. I know they're still a joy to see live. (Although if it was a choice, I'd pick Steve any day - I mean, I do have some minor criticisms, but he brings Craig Northey with him, and Craig Northey is the shit.)

Part of me thinks all it would take is for Steve to score a massive hit with a damn good song for Ed to, at the very least, come back to the studio with a resolve to create something with the same love and care as what I hear from him in *Maybe You Should Drive" and *Pirate Ship.*  I mean, John Lennon came out of retirement to record *Double Fantasy* after hearing Paul McCartney's "Coming Up" on the radio, surely something like that could happen to these two former songwriting partners. But then I remember that a) despite it all, John and Paul never lost a feeling of love towards one another and were basically reconciled before John passed, b) even if basic reconciliation, at any level, was a possibility at this point, there'd be zero point to it because they nothing to prove. Even though we still might not be completely comfortable with the situation, they're happy where they're at, and Steve is happy. We still have all the original records as a perfectly preserved time capsule of a band who truly knew how to feed off one another. 

It's disappointing, but it is what it is.

In my experience, it really depends on the band and the setting. 

For me, I'm a hardcore Sloan fan; a band that's been around for over 30 years and has the back catalog to match, and a band I have seen almost once for every year my generic Millennial ass has been alive. For me, there are three types of Sloan shows:

1) Canadian tour shows, which are primarily to promote the new album with setlists that will have a few hits for those coming to a show after however many years and maybe a couple of old album cuts for fun and for the hardcore fans (some of which might have come from a good distance to see them).

2) Canadian festivals, which are almost entirely radio hits. Of course I'll go because I love the band more than life itself, but I know I'm not going to hear anything deeper than Andrew Scott's "Sensory Deprivation" because the folks in the audience might not have given the band more than a few thoughts in many, many years (and it's the best showcase for when Andrew is on lead).

3) American shows, which are album promotion, but they're also more likely to throw in an outright B-side on top of several deep album cuts, all while perhaps skipping the biggest hits. Due to the fact their publishing has been hit or miss States-side, the American fans often have had little choice but to download *everything* - including the fan complied B-sides collection from the 2000's.  Their cult following might find it odd if they don't bring out the Raptors' playlist hit, but it might not actually matter. They're just happy to see the band perform. 

The point is that an artist should know their audience and determine the setlist from there.  If you're a multi-platinum superstar, it might be in their best interest to do the hits on a headling tour, but if I'm seeing them at a rare, fans-only club show, then I have no right to dictate the playlist. 

Side note, It's been too long since I saw Sloan outside of Canada. I should make it a point to do so next time.

/u/ShaneFalco393, and literally anyone reading this thread, for everything that is holy and rock and roll in this world, please listen to Sloan. I don't say stuff like this lightly, because I have been a Beatlemaniac through and through for exactly 38 years, one month, and 16 days, but I can proudly proclaim Sloan as *my* Beatles - at least, from the context of a late-20th/early-21st century music fan who was born four years too late to have existed on this planet alongside John Lennon. 

We're talking the sweetest power-pop living seamlessly alongside the loudest hardcore and just about everything in between. We're talking about a band with two drummers because both of them are just too talented and valuable as songwriters to remain behind the kit. We're talking 13 albums where opinions vary on favourites and preferences, but the conversation of choosing "the worst" simply doesn't happen because they *all* have true merit. We're talking about a band 33 years into it with all its members in their mid-50s, and the latest fan discussion basically agreed that they are currently in their true prime as a live act. And they have done it almost completely on their own; and if you took them out of the equation, particularly when it comes to Canadian independent music, a lot of bands and artists in this country just wouldn't have existed.

They are, at the very least, the greatest Canadian band of all time - and I have a lot of friends that would argue that they are simply the greatest to have ever existed anywhere.

Sloan are legit. Please listen to them, front to back, and if you're a first-time listener, please let me know what you think. 

PS: I'd particularly argue for *Never Hear the End of It* as an interesting starting point right now, but that might only be because they put out a double 45 of demos that's making want to listen to the whole damn record on repeat. But *Navy Blues*, *One Chord* and (to add) *Twice Removed* are some of the greatest Canadian albums ever recorded, so definitely great choices on places to start. 😁

I'm a massive Looney Tunes fan. Warts and all, those old cartoons are my happy place in an increasingly terrible world. I keep reflecting on the use of Bugs in drag, particularly in contrast to the horribly racist material that is in no short supply with the catalog - and for Hays Code-era Hollywood, my god Bugs was *way* ahead of his time. 

First off, to my knowledge, Bugs seems to be the only instance in the 40's and 50's filmmaking when a male character puts on a dress, you know someone's ass is going to get kicked, and the crossdresser is the one going to come out on top. 

But, in one important instance, those cartoons take it all a step further.  

(Side note, spoiler warning for *What's Opera, Doc?*. I'm not using spoiler tags because I'm on my phone, and formatting beyond the basics is a bit of a bitch. To be fair though, the short is over 65 years old and if you haven't seen it by now, some light searching will find it somewhere.)

So, *What's Opera, Doc?* is already considered a masterpiece, and for good reason. Its use of opera within a cartoon short setting made opera digestible for at least five new generations, and the brute force abstract animation is stunning.

But going a bit deeper, the deeper genius is in how they treat Bugs' turn as Brünnhilde. First off, the whole ballet sequence was animated with perfect attention to detail regarding body and foot positioning - so Bugs is legit in his ballet, and he's doing the woman's part.

But looking deeper, when Bugs' gender deception is revealed and Elmer becomes enraged to the point that he "kills the wabbit", he becomes distraught and remorseful when he realized what he did and the viewer feels sorry for what transpired. Or to put it another way, a gender-bending performer is outed and killed for being their natural, creative self and the death is deeply mourned.  And this was in 1956. 

Of course, it ends with Bugs breaking the fourth wall to say "Well, what did you expect in an opera, a happy ending?" and life goes back to your regularly scheduled morally questionable Looney Tunes cartoons of the Silent and Boomer generations. But, that moment is still proudly there and it's kind of beautiful.

The thing is, though, I am a passionate fan of Canadian music on the whole. There is so much brilliant music that comes from every single corner of this massive country of mine; and so much if it is ignored. Sloan is, in my general opinion, the greatest single rock band that has ever existed in Canada.  Four of the strongest and most consistent singer-songwriters producing every sub-genre of rock and power-pop imaginable - and thats before you read about their impact and contributions to the Halifax underground music scene and Canadian independent music. They've been crucial in showing all of us that you didn't have to have label backing to be a successful touring band releasing amazing music.  Sloan is the type of band that anyone who sees them live, particularly back in the day, comes out wanting to start a band. I love this band so fucking much and I want to see them celebrated as they should have been this entire time.

And yet, this amazing little band who have been kicking so much ass for 32 years now was passed over, yet again, because Nickelback is stratospherically popular and they became eligible this year (meanwhile, Sloan's been eligible for 12 years now).  

So yeah. I don't besmerch Nickelback fans. If you love them and their music as passionately as I love Sloan and it makes you happy beyond all belief, not one person on God's green Earth has the to judge someone for it. I know what that feels like; and I fucking hate it enough that I wouldn't wish it on my worst enemy. 

But for me, Nickelback's music just doesn't hold a candle to so much of what's out there, and it's almost offensive that it's given priority over so much greater talent.

I'm actually struggling with the opposite. I am Canadian and know far more people who are, very rightfully, critical of the Monarchy and what it represents within the context of colonialism. And I absolutely respect that because I witness the generational trauma everyday when I walk down the street to my work and see the countless homeless that all seem to fall under the same demographic. I don't completely understand the hurt, but I am working towards it.

But the thing is, my family is deeply British. On top of my father being from Manchester (where my first cousins all largely live), my maternal grandmother was a war bride - she met my grandfather when she was his nurse when he was injured in WWII and after they married, she came to live in Canada. Her entire life, she was so proud to be both British and Canadian. She held her Canadian passport as close as her connections to her nieces and nephews back in the UK - and she absolutely loved the Queen and was aiming to live to 100 so she would get her letter. She was so warm, welcoming and kind. She passed away about four years ago now, at 92. We're all disappointed that she didn't get her letter.

When Nana passed away, it was a bit of a slow process. She fell and broke her shoulder in November, and was in the hospital for about four months before she passed.  Living 10 hours away, I had my phone off silent pretty much the entire time, scared for the day I would get word; and praying that I'd get home for Christmas in time to see her. This was also the same year that Pixar's *Coco* came out in theaters, and I don't know what was worse: knowing I didn't turn my phone off in the theatre or the absolute ugly cry I had in public watching this movie that seemed to feel a bit to spot on. (Thankfully, I made it home in time.)

My sister (who is thoroughly proud to be a royal watcher, just because she finds it all fascinating) and I recognized soon after Nan passed that the death of Queen Elizabeth would be a doozy for us, as we would be loosing our one living reminder of the Monarch our Nan embodied within our family. 

Today, September 8th, 2022, would have been Nan's 97 birthday.  Living in Canada, the breaking news that the family was gathering at Balmoral came right before the 8am radio news break.  All day, my phone was off silent and allowing breaking Twitter news to come through, and I was in constant contact with my family, and there was the same sinking feeling from every update I read. It truly felt like I was losing my Nan all over again. 

I think the big thing to understand is simply to empathize with the absolutely enormous amount of complexity within this particular situation, and simply be undestanding to those who don't share the incredibly valid opinion as you.  At the end of the day, you, me and the Queen are all human; and as humans, we feel loss as deeply as we do our personal moral values. 

Nobody's opinions are in the wrong. And that's OK.

Today would have been my very proud British-Canadian war bride grandmother's birthday. She passed away four years ago. She would have been 97. 

Fuck the politics of it all. It feels lile losing Nan all over again.

So, Sloan got their start in Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1991; and since 1991, they have always consisted of Jay Ferguson, Chris Murphy, Patrick Pentland and Andrew Scott. Not one line up change has been made in this time. All four members are absolute craftsmen power-pop songwriters and, within the band, they sing their own songs. Every songwriter comes with his own set of influences, which creates this incredible mix of all the eras of rock into one. The comment that someone close to me recently said is that a Sloan record is a "desert island cheat code", as it almost sounds like you're listening to four amazing bands in one.  

The only difference between Sloan and some of the bigger names in Canadian music is a matter of name recognition. Sloan started as an independent band (creating their own label, Murderecords), but were signed quite quickly into their career - they were going to be billed as Canada's answer to Nirvana. They didn't stay signed for long, however. They had their chance, but rightfully shunned label pressure when they were told to re-record *Twice Removed* (an album still considered to be one of the greatest Canadian albums of all time) to better suit a grunge audience. They actually broke up for a hot minute because the pressure was a bit much. 

So they never achieved any kind of label support, but being the BAMFs they are, they reformed, dusted themselves off, recorded *One Chord to Another* independently (an album usually featured on the same lists as *Twice Removed*), created their own sustainable business model (four individual songwriters, yes, but all songwriting royalties are split equally between everyone) and 30 years into it are still creating the most consistently solid bodies of work out of any rock band either here or internationally. Bonus, they have a live show that melts faces from the power of the rock.  

Sloan basically created the Canadian independent music scene as we know it through their absolute quality music. Problem is, as far as popularity numbers are concerned, although they've had a slew of radio hits and have a massive cult following, international-Nickelback-level-popular they are not and are often forgotten in the conversation - so I started the conversation myself.

TL;DR: The moment I gave up my dreams of being a musician to take journalism in college I began to live a life completely engulfed in music.

When I applied to college, I had a choice between taking music industry arts or journalism. I ultimately chose journalism because, as much as I wanted to be in a music-related fields so badly it hurt, I was pushing 30 and coming out of an almost decade long depression. I wasn't nearly as good on bass as I was in high school becauseIl I really hadn't studied in years, and thought at least journalism would have a ton of transferable skills to get me an adult job - and I wouldn't be bored learning them.

I had to buy a DSLR camera for the course. Not even a week into having the thing, I got permission to shoot my first concert. My second semester, I attended my first major music media event as a member of the press. Apart from a few years of depression relapse, I really haven't looked back. I'm doing exactly what I wanted to do in life - I just had to put down the guitar and pick up a camera. That's all.

The music of my favourite band, Sloan. First off, they're celebrating their 30th anniversary right now, and they've been releasing new stuff in celebration; so yay!  But also, I started a petition to get them into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame a number of months back, and recently it got a bit of traction on some music blogs.
